title: The Grid: A Journey Through the Heart of Our Electrified World
author: Phillip F. Schewe
note: An explanatory history for general readers, not a technical curriculum or routine institutional report. No serious veto established. Its useful payload concerns network interdependence, supply-demand balancing, AC transmission, utility institutions and failure propagation. The primary setting is the United States, so T11 applies; electricity infrastructure is the central topic, so T12 does not. The historical account reaches the early 2000s and pre-publication present; 2006 is the assessed endpoint. Publisher and library records support 2007; Goodreads gives December 2006, an unresolved advance-publication discrepancy. Use the publisher's original year, not the later paperback date.
notes: Sourced historical explanation by an AIP science writer; Brennan identifies an incomplete treatment of California's regulatory design. This limits causal confidence without establishing failure of the central infrastructure account.
Connects electricity generation and transmission to network reliability, utility organization, investment and social dependence.
Transferable lessons concern coupled systems, reliability, scale and the institutional conditions needed for infrastructure operation.
Explains AC transmission and cascading failure, but gives less complete regulatory causation and technical detail than an engineering history could.

D=7/10, moderate confidence from the contents and named independent reviews, not full-text coverage. AC/DC history, Insull's utility system, blackout propagation and transformer repair add distinct learning. Repeated literary reflection and the late Apollo comparison are reported lower-yield material; their effect is separate from technical-depth limitations.
Historical engineering and reliability lessons remain useful; its account of contemporary supply technology is dated.
Electrical infrastructure, large engineered networks and reliability directly fit the requested domains.
Schewe is a physicist and AIP science writer; a specialist electricity-economics review provides substantive external scrutiny.
Accessible episodes and memorable failures; the independent review notes distracting flourishes and a nonlinear organization.
Generally clear explanation, with literary embellishment that sometimes reduces precision.
